title: Maritime Psychology: Definition, Scope and Conceptualization
central_proposition: This paper defines maritime psychology, outlines its scope, and proposes a systems-based conceptualization of the maritime transport industry to integrate organizational, social, and health psychology research, emphasizing the critical role of psychosocial factors and the 'human element' in maritime safety and well-being.

concept_definitions.name: Maritime psychology
concept_definitions.definition: the study and practice of the interplay between human behaviour and the maritime environment.

concept_definitions.name: Human element
concept_definitions.definition: the “marinized” term used to describe at least some of the aspects of psychology

concept_definitions.name: Safety culture
concept_definitions.definition: how people behave when no one is looking.

concept_definitions.name: Psychological capital (PsyCap)
concept_definitions.definition: an individual’s positive psychological state of development and is characterized by: (1) having confidence (self-efficacy) to take on and put in the necessary effort to succeed at challenging tasks; (2) making a positive attribution (optimism) about succeeding now and in the future; (3) persevering towards goals and, when necessary, redirecting paths to goals (hope) in order to succeed; and (4) when beset by problems and adversity, sustaining and bouncing back and even beyond (resiliency) to attain success

concept_definitions.name: Resilience
concept_definitions.definition: the ability to “bounce back” from adversity

concept_definitions.name: Positive psychology
concept_definitions.definition: a science of positive subjective experience, positive individual traits, and positive institutions (which) promises to improve quality of life” and prevent pathologies

concept_definitions.name: Positive organizational psychology (POP)
concept_definitions.definition: the scientific study of positive subjective experiences and traits in the workplace and positive institutions

concept_definitions.name: Positive organizational scholarship (POS)
concept_definitions.definition: focuses on the study of positive outcomes, processes, and attributes of organizations and their members

concept_definitions.name: Positive organizational behaviour (POB)
concept_definitions.definition: concerned with the study of individual positive psy chological conditions and human resource strengths that are related to employee well-being or performance improvement

concept_definitions.name: Occupational stress
concept_definitions.definition: a term which is often used in the scientific literature and in daily life. However, there is no general agreement on its definition

concept_definitions.name: Stress (Lazarus & Folkman)
concept_definitions.definition: a relationship between the individual and the environment arising from the former’s estimation that the requirements of the latter exceed his capabilities to meet them.

concept_definitions.name: Healthy organization
concept_definitions.definition: one whose culture, management, working climate and other business practices create an environment that promotes the complete physical, mental and social well-being, effectiveness and performance of its employees

concept_definitions.name: Motion sickness
concept_definitions.definition: the generally accepted explanation of the ‘how’ of motion sickness, i.e. the mechanism, is based on some form of sensory conflict or sensory mismatch between actual versus expected invariant patterns of vestibular, visual, and kinaesthetic inputs as predicted by an ‘internal model’

concept_definitions.name: Mal-de-debarquement
concept_definitions.definition: the sensation of unsteadiness and tilting of the ground

concept_definitions.name: Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM)
concept_definitions.definition: investigates the different ways that people process communication messages, and the different results for communication effectiveness, including changes in attitude or behaviour, such as compliance or rejection.

concept_definitions.name: Central processing (ELM)
concept_definitions.definition: attitudes are formed as a result of careful assessment of a range of information

concept_definitions.name: Peripheral processing (ELM)
concept_definitions.definition: attitudes are adopted more rapidly and in a less considered way

concept_definitions.name: Ecopsychology
concept_definitions.definition: human evolution—in particular our “moving away from nature”—that is at least in part responsible for some health, and particularly mental health, problems.

concept_definitions.name: Ecotherapy
concept_definitions.definition: building a relationship with nature, so that personal wellbeing is considered equally alongside the health of the environment

argument_structure: The paper begins by defining maritime psychology and outlining its broad scope across commercial, recreational, environmental, intervention, military, and safety domains. It then focuses on commercial shipping, detailing the importance of psychosocial factors and the 'human element'. A nested systems model (Fig. 1, p. 21) is introduced to illustrate the multi-level interactions (individual, team, organization, business, industry). Subsequent sections explore specific challenges and opportunities within maritime psychology, such as ship evacuation, piracy, organizational culture, psychological capital, and global health. The paper concludes by previewing the empirical chapters in the volume, which exemplify these theoretical concepts.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core causal logic posits that the unique and demanding maritime environment, encompassing physical, social, and organizational factors, directly influences seafarers' psychological states, health, and performance. These individual-level outcomes, in turn, aggregate to impact team and organizational safety and efficiency. The paper argues that interventions, whether psychological (e.g., positive psychology, resilience training), architectural (e.g., human-centered design), or communicative (e.g., risk communication strategies), can modulate these relationships. For instance, sensory conflicts lead to motion sickness, while effective communication can mitigate risks. A systems perspective is crucial, as changes at one level (e.g., individual coping) interact with and are influenced by other levels (e.g., organizational culture, industry regulations).

findings.antecedent: Psychosocial factors in the maritime field
findings.consequent: Well-being, health, and performance of seafarers, and maritime safety
findings.mechanism: Psychosocial factors (e.g., social isolation, confinement, multicultural crews, workload, fatigue, stress) directly influence the mental and physical state of seafarers, impacting their ability to perform tasks safely and efficiently.
findings.quote: The importance of psychosocial factors is being increasingly recognized in the maritime field
findings.empirical_support_cited: The importance of psychosocial factors is being increasingly recognised in the maritime field

findings.mechanism: The unique characteristics of the maritime environment, such as isolation, confinement, and safety-critical operations, create specific stressors (e.g., long work hours, sleep deprivation, social isolation, limited recreation) that impact seafarers' psychological and physical health, and their ability to perform.
findings.source: Positive Psychology and Well-Being at Sea, p. 33-34
findings.quote: The ship as an isolated, confined environment—comprising the people, settings, tasks, amenities, and routines to which seafarers may be exposed for weeks and some times months at a time.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Seafaring has long combined paradoxes, such as social exclusion and continuous social proximity, confinement in open spaces, and multiculturalism, within the single organizational culture of a ship.

findings.antecedent: Positive psychology interventions (e.g., gratitude diary, using signature strengths, meditation, writing about life goals)
findings.mechanism: These interventions cultivate positive subjective experiences, build positive individual traits (e.g., hope, resilience, optimism, self-efficacy), and foster civic virtue, leading to enhanced psychological capital, improved coping skills, and better overall functioning in demanding maritime contexts.
findings.source: Chapters in This Volume, p. 25; Positive Psychology, p. 39
findings.quote: Positive psychology interventions may be elucidated as intentional activities based on (a) cultivation of positive subjective experiences; (b) building of positive individual traits; or (c) building of civic virtue and positive institutions
findings.empirical_support_cited: Generally, these studies indicate that relatively modest, or even small-scale, interventions can have quite positive effects, often on well-being and performance, across a range of work environments.

findings.antecedent: High levels of psychological capital (hope, resiliency, optimism, self-efficacy)
findings.consequent: Positive perception of safety climate, job satisfaction, organizational effectiveness, positive work outcomes
findings.mechanism: Psychological capital acts as a positive reserve of value, enhancing individuals' motivational states and their ability to cope with challenges, leading to more positive appraisals of their work environment and greater engagement.
findings.source: Psychological Capital, p. 23; Positive Psychology and Well-Being at Sea, p. 43
findings.quote: Psychological capital may be an important factor concerning seafarers’ safety climate.
findings.empirical_support_cited: This motivational state has been shown to be related to organizational effectiveness and positive work outcomes (Newman et al. 2014), and has recently been explored in the maritime environment by Bergheim et al. (2015).

findings.antecedent: Systems-based approach to maritime health interventions (considering environmental, organizational, operational, safety, and cultural aspects)
findings.consequent: Integrated health care interventions, comprehensive approach to maritime health
findings.mechanism: A systems approach recognizes the complex interplay of various factors influencing seafarers' health and performance, allowing for more holistic and effective interventions that address root causes rather than just symptoms.
findings.source: Global Health at Work, p. 51; Conclusion, p. 52
findings.quote: a systems-based perspective that addresses safety, cultural, environmental, operational and organi zational aspects can ensure a more comprehensive approach to maritime health.
findings.empirical_support_cited: A systems approach to managing stressors is the basis of the Crew Endurance Management System

findings.antecedent: Transfer of learning across safety-critical industries (e.g., aviation to maritime)
findings.consequent: Improved safety management systems, enhanced human factors capacity
findings.mechanism: By systematically profiling sectors, identifying challenges, and adapting successful solutions (e.g., CRM/BRM, HF training) from more mature safety cultures, the 'arrival' sector can progress towards proactive safety management and continuous improvement.
findings.source: Transferring Learning Across Safety-Critical Industries, p. 50, 62
findings.quote: The SEAHORSE project is a research and development project funded by the EU which aims to transfer safety technology from the aviation sector to the maritime sector.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The drivers for transfer are discussed and the two dominant existing approaches to transfer are detailed.

findings.antecedent: Ship architecture and design (e.g., living/working spaces, physical environment)
findings.consequent: Seafarers' sleep quality, fatigue, privacy, attitudes to safety, crew turnover, social structure, psychological experience
findings.mechanism: The physical characteristics of the ship (size, layout, materials, noise, vibration) directly influence the comfort, functionality, and social dynamics of the onboard environment, which in turn affects seafarers' physiological and psychological states.
findings.source: The Psychology of Ship Architecture and Design, p. 26
findings.quote: The physical environment also dramatically influences sleep quality, fatigue and opportunities for privacy
findings.empirical_support_cited: Given that a ship is a space at sea that people live in, the characteristics of that space are likely to have significant effects of the behaviour of seafarers.

findings.antecedent: Lack of appropriate Human Factors (HF) consideration in ship design
findings.consequent: Poorer operations, higher training costs, increased risk of failing at tasks, 'operator error'
findings.mechanism: Excluding human factors from the design process leads to systems that are not optimized for human capabilities and limitations, resulting in design-induced errors, increased workload, and reduced safety and efficiency.
findings.source: The Psychology of Ship Architecture and Design, p. 84
findings.quote: Insufficient integration of HF in design may translate into poorer operations, higher training costs, and an increased risk of failing at the task
findings.empirical_support_cited: It has been estimated that 60–80 % of all accidents at sea are the result of “operator error”

findings.antecedent: Design engineers' natural inclinations (object-world thinking, decomposition, numerical expression, distant relationship to end-users)
findings.consequent: Insufficient consideration of human factors and psychology of ship design
findings.mechanism: The inherent cognitive biases and training of design engineers lead them to prioritize technical and measurable aspects over qualitative human-centered requirements, resulting in designs that do not fully meet end-user needs.
findings.source: The Psychology of Ship Architecture and Design, p. 89
findings.quote: design engineers are not naturally inclined towards the “softness” of the psychology of ship design.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The remainder of this section will elaborate on how and why design engineers are not naturally inclined towards the “softness” of the psychology of ship design.

findings.antecedent: Occupational stressors in seafaring (e.g., long separation from home, poor living/working conditions, high workload, multinational crews, job insecurity)
findings.consequent: Physical and psychological health problems (e.g., depression, anxiety, fatigue, burnout, heart disease, suicide), decreased job satisfaction, reduced performance, increased accidents
findings.mechanism: Chronic exposure to multiple stressors in the demanding maritime environment leads to allostatic load, psychological distress, and physiological dysregulation, impairing seafarers' well-being and increasing the risk of adverse health and safety outcomes.
findings.quote: Occupational stressors have been implicated as risk factors for many physical, psychological and behavioural problems in workers
findings.empirical_support_cited: Seafaring is a demanding, high-risk and stressful occupation which cannot be compared with jobs ashore.

findings.antecedent: Fatigue (progressive loss of mental and physical alertness)
findings.consequent: Impaired cognition, reduced performance, increased accident risk, chronic health effects (e.g., sleep disorders, cardiovascular diseases, metabolic syndrome, psychiatric conditions)
findings.mechanism: Fatigue, especially when chronic or related to shift work and sleep deprivation, disrupts circadian rhythms, impairs cognitive functions (attention, decision-making), and leads to physiological dysregulation, increasing the likelihood of errors, accidents, and long-term health problems.
findings.source: Risk Factors for Fatigue in Shipping, p. 139-140
findings.quote: Work-related fatigue is particularly an issue in safety-sensitive occupational sectors
findings.empirical_support_cited: Fatigue in a health sense represents a state of physical and/or mental duress that can affect any person, regardless of occupation or cultural background.

findings.antecedent: Sensory conflict or sensory mismatch (between actual vs. expected vestibular, visual, and kinaesthetic inputs)
findings.mechanism: The brain's internal model predicts sensory inputs based on expected patterns. When actual inputs conflict with these predictions, a 'prediction error' or 'sensory mismatch' occurs, triggering the motion sickness response as a defense mechanism (e.g., toxin detector hypothesis).
findings.source: How Do the Mechanisms for Motion Sickness Work?, p. 167; Why Should Motion Sickness Exist at All?, p. 171
findings.quote: The poison or toxin detector hypothesis states that the vestibular system can act as a toxin detector.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The generally accepted explanation of the ‘how’ of motion sickness, i.e. the mechanism, is based on some form of sensory conflict or sensory mismatch between actual versus expected invariant patterns of vestibular, visual, and kinaesthetic inputs as predicted by an ‘internal model’

findings.mechanism: Controlled breathing may activate protective inhibitory reflexes between respiration and vomiting, providing a non-pharmacological countermeasure to motion sickness.
findings.source: Non-pharmacological Countermeasures Against Motion Sickness, p. 182
findings.quote: Controlled regular breathing has been shown to increase motion tolerance to provocative motion
findings.empirical_support_cited: Controlled regular breathing has been shown to increase motion tolerance to provocative motion, being approximately half as effective as standard anti-motion sickness drugs yet rapid to implement and free of side effects

findings.antecedent: Motion sickness susceptibility (individual differences, genetics, age, gender, aerobic fitness, mood)
findings.consequent: Likelihood and severity of motion sickness
findings.mechanism: Individual variations in genetic predispositions, physiological reactivity, developmental stages, and psychological states (e.g., anxiety, arousal) influence the sensitivity of the sensory conflict detection system and the threshold for triggering motion sickness symptoms.
findings.source: Predictors of Motion Sickness Susceptibility, p. 173; Genetics, p. 175
findings.quote: Monozygotic and dizygotic twin studies suggest that the heritability of motion sickness is high at around 70 % in childhood
findings.empirical_support_cited: Determinants of motion sickness susceptibility are doubtless multifactorial.

findings.consequent: Psychological consequences (e.g., PTSD, psychological distress, secondary traumatic stress, stress, fear, anxiety, blaming, anger, fatigue, dissociation)
findings.mechanism: Exposure to traumatic events, especially human-made disasters, can overwhelm individuals' coping mechanisms, leading to a range of acute and chronic psychological reactions that impact their mental health and ability to process information.
findings.source: Review of State of the Knowledge, p. 197
findings.quote: The psychological reactions to such an event may be plotted on a continuum.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The impact of disasters such as those outlined previously is far reaching and may have psychological consequences for some of the people involved.

findings.consequent: Message processing (central vs. peripheral route), attitude/behavioral change, compliance/rejection
findings.mechanism: According to ELM, the effectiveness of communication depends on the audience's motivation and ability to elaborate. Central processing (facts, logic) leads to lasting change, while peripheral processing (cues like credibility, likeability, visuals) leads to temporary shifts, especially for stressed or unmotivated audiences.
findings.source: The Implications for Communication Practice, p. 198-199
findings.quote: Messages processed by the central route usually result in long-lasting attitude or behavioural change
findings.empirical_support_cited: Developed by social psychologists Petty and Cacioppo (1986), ELM investigates the different ways that people process communication messages

findings.antecedent: Sailing as an intervention (e.g., sail training, therapeutic sailing)
findings.consequent: Self-development, social and emotional skills, self-confidence, self-image, well-being, physical/cognitive skills, rehabilitation, social inclusion
findings.mechanism: The unique maritime environment, especially in structured programs, provides challenges and opportunities for teamwork, skill acquisition, and personal reflection, fostering psychological growth, improved physical and cognitive functioning, and a sense of purpose and connection.
findings.quote: Our voyage crew develop self-confidence, self-image and positive results.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The Jubilee Sailing Trust (JST) registered as a charity in 1978 with the aim of integrating people with physical disabilities with non-disabled people in an enjoyable activity.

findings.antecedent: Cynicism and mistrust towards others (personality traits of Greek merchant marine officers)
findings.mechanism: These personality characteristics, potentially 'attracted' by seafaring or induced by organizational factors, lead to a perception of others' motives with skepticism, hindering deep social connections and fostering a sense of detachment.
findings.quote: a possible hypothesis would be that although our group is free from problems related to socializing, they perceive the motives of the people they come across with scepticism, if not distrust (or even mistrust).
findings.empirical_support_cited: The higher scores in RC3 and RC6 have also been linked to alienation.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Do positive psychology interventions and training enhance well-being, performance and safety in the workplace, and through what mechanisms do these interventions and training operate? Are these mechanisms transferable to the maritime environment?
What are the facilitators and barriers to the effective implementation of positive psychology interventions that are specific to the maritime context?
Do positive psychology interventions show signs of effect maintenance in the maritime context?
Do positive psychology interventions present any advantages or disadvantages relative to other forms of psychological intervention in the maritime context?
How can positive psychology interventions and training be designed and administered to be accessible across ranks, sexes, ages, cultures and ethnicities on board?
Are positive psychology computer-based interventions and training an effective and viable option in the maritime context?
How can a systems-based approach to research and implementation be designed to facilitate integrated health care interventions in the maritime environment?
Can design make safety, efficiency and satisfaction?
If ships were built by engineers with non-technical skills, would that make a difference?

What distinguishes sailing as an intervention compared to other types of outdoor interventions? And related to this, is sailing simply a variation in the outdoors that may be more attractive to some than to others, or is there an element of engaging with the maritime that makes it qualitatively different from other outdoor interventions?
what is the optimal type of structure to bestow the greatest benefit for participants?
If there are benefits associated with sailing for such interventions, are they similar for the two types of interventions; are there commonalities, but also distinctive mechanisms in each case?
what are the possible mechanisms of benefit here? (referring to corporate sailing interventions)
to what extent sailing can be offered more widely as an intervention.
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly connects the 'human element' in maritime to psychological aspects.
It draws parallels between aviation safety management (CRM) and maritime (BRM), suggesting transfer of learning.
It links occupational stress in seafaring to general occupational stress models (Lazarus & Folkman).
It applies the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) from social psychology to maritime risk communication.
It connects sailing as an intervention to 'outdoor experiential learning' and 'ecopsychology'.
It uses the STAMINA model (aviation human factors) as a framework for sector analysis in maritime.
It discusses the 'toxin detector hypothesis' for motion sickness, linking it to evolutionary maladaptation.
methodological_critiques: Existing maritime psychology research is often 'piecemeal, opportunistic and of modest scale'.
Many studies on occupational stress in seafaring are based only on questionnaire surveys conducted ashore, lacking objective measurements.
Self-report studies of stress often suffer from common method variance and negative affectivity.
Longitudinal research and qualitative approaches (interviews, focus groups) are needed to capture dynamic changes and less-explored issues.
MMPI-2 studies in seafaring are limited in sample size, single company, limited demographic data, and financial crisis context.
Online interventions need to consider highly restricted internet access on board.
Transfer of learning across safety-critical industries is challenging due to sector differences.
The effectiveness of in-practice training for ship designers is yet to be seen.
The application of full-scope HCD by design engineering is unlikely to be successful due to the maritime industry's usability capability maturity level.
Research on sailing as an intervention is in its infancy, often piecemeal and opportunistic.
The perception of sailing as elitist, costly, and dangerous acts as a barrier to access.
The 'frame' of therapy rooms is lost in outdoor settings, requiring re-negotiation of confidentiality, comfort, and consistency.
ELM has weaknesses, being difficult to test and failing to produce clear guidelines on strong/weak arguments.
Psychometric assessment instruments should be based on validity and reliability, and not used as single measures for selection.
Current fatigue prediction models do not include individual and task variables, and user interface has limited user friendliness.
Research on motion sickness susceptibility often lacks robust physiological markers.
The efficacy of anti-motion sickness drugs is limited by side effects and absorption delays.
Habituation to motion sickness can be stimulus-specific and slow to acquire.
Design engineering curriculum is biased towards technological subjects, lacking human factors.
Design engineers are not naturally inclined towards 'softness' of psychology, prioritizing objects and decomposition.
The 'human element' is a 'marinized' term for psychology, suggesting a lack of explicit psychological recognition.
model_structure: The paper proposes a nested model of psychosocial and organizational aspects of maritime work (Fig. 1, p. 21), which integrates the STAMINA model of human factors across five hierarchical levels: Task, Individual, Team, Organization, and Industry. Each level is embedded within the next, and all levels are understood to interact dynamically. Additionally, a structured methodology for transferring learning and innovation (STEM) is outlined, comprising three steps: Comparison, Match, and Adaptation and Implementation (p. 62). For ship design, an iterative Human-Centred Design (HCD) approach, adapted for a 'low-key' application, is presented (Fig. 3, p. 103), focusing on simplified context understanding, solution generation, and evaluation.
limitations: The volume is not exhaustive or comprehensive in covering maritime psychology.
The primary focus is on commercial maritime transport, not other maritime activities.
The definition of maritime psychology is expected to be contested and evolve.
Modelling human behavior under extreme stress (ship evacuation) is complex and difficult to predict.
Psychological interventions in an unfair/exploitive working environment can be counterproductive.
The scope of psychology in the commercial transport sector remains underdeveloped.
The MMPI-2 study has limitations: small sample size, single company, limited demographic data, and financial crisis context.
Online interventions need to consider highly restricted internet access on board.
Transfer of learning across safety-critical industries is challenging due to sector differences.
The effectiveness of in-practice training for ship designers is yet to be seen.
The application of full-scope HCD by design engineering is unlikely to be successful due to the maritime industry's usability capability maturity level.
Research on sailing as an intervention is in its infancy, often piecemeal and opportunistic.
The perception of sailing as elitist, costly, and dangerous acts as a barrier to access.
The 'frame' of therapy rooms is lost in outdoor settings, requiring re-negotiation of confidentiality, comfort, and consistency.
ELM has weaknesses, being difficult to test and failing to produce clear guidelines on strong/weak arguments.
